# Esther Chapter 4 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Source Manuscript:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folio 457r-457v | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/EST_004_page_001.jpg

---

## Consensus Translation

**4:1** When Mordecai learned all that had been done, he tore his garments, put on sackcloth and ashes, and went out into the city, crying out with a loud and bitter cry.

**4:2** He went as far as the entrance to the king's gate, for no one was permitted to enter the king's gate clothed in sackcloth.

**4:3** In every province, wherever the king's command and decree reached, there was great mourning among the Jews — fasting, weeping, and lamentation. Many lay on sackcloth and ashes.

**4:4** When Esther's attendants and eunuchs came and told her, the queen was deeply distressed. She sent garments for Mordecai to wear so he could remove his sackcloth, but he refused.

**4:5** Then Esther summoned Hathach, one of the king's eunuchs appointed to attend her, and sent him to Mordecai to learn what was happening and why.

**4:6** Hathach went out to Mordecai in the open square of the city before the king's gate.

**4:7** Mordecai told him everything that had happened, including the exact amount of silver Haman had promised to pay into the royal treasury for the destruction of the Jews.

**4:8** He also gave him a copy of the written decree issued in Susa for their destruction, to show it to Esther and explain it to her, and to urge her to go to the king, to implore his mercy, and to plead before him on behalf of her people.

**4:9** Hathach returned and reported Mordecai's words to Esther.

**4:10** Then Esther spoke to Hathach and gave him a message for Mordecai:

**4:11** "All the king's servants and the people of the king's provinces know that for any man or woman who enters the inner court without being summoned, there is but one law: death — unless the king extends the golden scepter and spares that person's life. And I have not been summoned to come before the king for thirty days."

**4:12** When Mordecai was told what Esther had said,

**4:13** he sent back this reply: "Do not imagine that because you are in the king's palace you will escape any more than the rest of the Jews.

**4:14** For if you remain silent at this time, relief and deliverance will arise for the Jews from another place, but you and your father's house will perish. And who knows whether you have not come to the kingdom for such a time as this?"

**4:15** Then Esther sent this reply to Mordecai:

**4:16** "Go, gather all the Jews who are in Susa, and fast on my behalf. Do not eat or drink for three days, night or day. I and my attendants will fast in the same way. Then I will go to the king, though it is against the law. And if I perish, I perish."

**4:17** So Mordecai went and did everything Esther had commanded him.

---

## SOPHIA's Council Notes

Chapter 4 is the theological and dramatic center of the book of Esther. The council recognized unanimously that Mordecai's words in verse 14 — "relief and deliverance will arise for the Jews from another place" — constitute the closest the book comes to naming God, and that this near-naming is deliberate and powerful. The phrase *mimaqom acher* ("from another place") has been understood by Jewish tradition as a veiled reference to God; the rabbinic designation of God as *HaMaqom* ("The Place") reinforces this reading. Esther's transformation in this chapter is equally significant: she moves from passive obedience to active command, calling a communal fast and accepting mortal risk with the words "if I perish, I perish." The council noted that in verse 17, for the first time, Mordecai obeys Esther rather than the reverse — a quiet but momentous reversal of their relationship that mirrors the larger reversals the book is building toward.

---

## Disagreement Log

**1. Verse 4:1 — Intensity of Mordecai's cry**
- EMET: "cried out [vayyiz'aq] a great [gedolah] and bitter [umarah] cry [ze'aqah]" — literal, preserving each adjective.
- LOGOS: "crying out with a loud and bitter cry" — formal equivalent.
- PNEUMA: "wailing with a piercing, agonized cry" — interpretive intensification.
- SOPHIA ruling: Adopted LOGOS phrasing. The Hebrew adjectives are *gedolah* (great/loud) and *marah* (bitter). PNEUMA's "piercing" and "agonized" are vivid but go beyond the semantic range of the Hebrew. LOGOS accurately captures both dimensions — volume and emotional quality.

**2. Verse 4:14 — "from another place" phrasing**
- EMET: "from another place [mimaqom acher]" — literal.
- LOGOS: "from another place" — identical to EMET.
- PNEUMA: "from somewhere else" — colloquial paraphrase.
- SOPHIA ruling: Adopted "from another place" (EMET/LOGOS consensus). The Hebrew *maqom* is theologically significant — it is a rabbinic name for God (*HaMaqom*). PNEUMA's "somewhere else" loses this resonance entirely. The more formal "from another place" preserves the possibility that the attentive reader will hear the theological undertone.

**3. Verse 4:16 — "if I perish, I perish" vs. "if I die, I die"**
- EMET: "if I perish [avadeti], I perish [avadeti]" — using "perish" for the Hebrew *avad*.
- LOGOS: "if I perish, I perish" — same as EMET.
- PNEUMA: "If I die, I die" — simpler, more direct.
- SOPHIA ruling: Adopted "if I perish, I perish" (EMET/LOGOS). The Hebrew *avad* means "to perish, to be destroyed, to be lost" — a stronger and more comprehensive term than simply "die." The same root appears in Haman's decree (3:13, *le'abbed*, "to annihilate"), creating a verbal link: Esther accepts the very fate decreed against her people. PNEUMA's "die" loses this connection.

**4. Verse 4:17 — Reversal of authority**
- EMET: "did according to all that Esther had commanded him [tzivvetah alav]" — preserves the verb *tzivvah* (command).
- LOGOS: "did everything Esther had commanded him" — equivalent.
- PNEUMA: "carried out everything Esther had told him to do" — uses "told" instead of "commanded."
- SOPHIA ruling: Adopted "did everything Esther had commanded him" (LOGOS). The Hebrew *tzivvah* specifically means "to command," not merely "to tell." PNEUMA's softening of the verb obscures the deliberate reversal: earlier, Mordecai *commanded* Esther (2:10, 2:20); now Esther *commands* Mordecai. The word must be the same to make the reversal audible.

---

*— SOPHIA, in council with EMET, LOGOS, and PNEUMA*
